910.name: Ancient Phoenicia
910.description: The Phoenician city-states of Byblos, Sidon, and Tyre — master mariners and traders who invented the alphabet, colonized the Mediterranean, and supplied cedarwood to the ancient world.

sub_clusters.name: Early Byblos and Egyptian Ties
sub_clusters.description: Byblos as one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities, its deep trade links with Egypt, the export of Lebanese cedar for shipbuilding and temples, and the development of the Phoenician alphabet.
key_events: Byblos becomes a major exporter of cedar and papyrus to Egypt (c. 2800 BC)
The Phoenician alphabet develops — ancestor of virtually all modern alphabets (c. 1050 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Tyre, Sidon, and Mediterranean Expansion
sub_clusters.description: The golden age of Tyre and Sidon after the Bronze Age Collapse, Phoenician colonization of Carthage, trade in Tyrian purple dye, King Hiram's alliance with Solomon, and the Assyrian and Babylonian subjugations.
key_events: Phoenicians found Carthage from Tyre (814 BC)
Alexander the Great besieges and captures Tyre, building a causeway to the island city (332 BC)

910.name: Hellenistic and Roman Lebanon
910.description: Lebanon under Seleucid, Roman, and Byzantine rule, the splendor of Roman Berytus and its famous law school, the monumental temples of Baalbek, and the spread of Christianity.

sub_clusters.name: Seleucid and Roman Berytus
sub_clusters.description: The Hellenization of Phoenician cities, Roman colonization of Berytus (Beirut), the construction of the legendary Baalbek temples, and Berytus' renowned law school that shaped Roman jurisprudence.
key_events: Construction of the great Temple of Jupiter at Baalbek — largest Roman temple complex (1st–3rd century AD)
Berytus law school becomes one of the three great law schools of the Roman Empire

sub_clusters.name: Early Christianity and Byzantine Period
sub_clusters.description: The early spread of Christianity in Phoenician cities, the Maronite community's formation around Saint Maron, Mount Lebanon's monastic traditions, and the devastating earthquake of 551.
key_events: Earthquake and tsunami destroy Berytus and its law school (551 AD)

920.name: Early Islamic Period and Crusader States
920.description: The Arab conquest and islamization of coastal Lebanon, the refuge communities of Mount Lebanon, and the dramatic Crusader period with its fortified cities and battles.

sub_clusters.name: Arab Conquest and Mount Lebanon Communities
sub_clusters.description: The Rashidun conquest of the Levant, the Umayyad and Abbasid periods, the Maronites' retreat into Mount Lebanon, and the arrival of the Druze community.
key_events: Battle of Yarmouk — Arab forces defeat Byzantines, opening the Levant to Islam (636 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Crusader County of Tripoli
sub_clusters.description: The establishment of the County of Tripoli, Crusader fortresses like Krak des Chevaliers on Lebanon's borders, Maronite alliance with the Crusaders and union with Rome, and the Mamluk reconquest.
key_events: Raymond of Saint-Gilles besieges and captures Tripoli, founding the Crusader county (1109)
Mamluks capture the last Crusader strongholds on the Lebanese coast (1289–1291)

920.name: Mamluk and Early Ottoman Lebanon
920.description: Mount Lebanon under Mamluk suzerainty, the transition to Ottoman rule, and the emergence of the Druze Ma'n dynasty as local power brokers.

sub_clusters.name: Mamluk Period
sub_clusters.description: The Mamluk Sultanate's control of coastal Lebanon, the autonomy of the mountain communities, Maronite and Druze coexistence, and the continuation of trade through Beirut and Tripoli.

sub_clusters.name: Early Ottoman Period and Ma'n Dynasty
sub_clusters.description: The Ottoman conquest of the Levant, the Druze Ma'n emirs' role as Ottoman-appointed governors of Mount Lebanon, and the foundations of the Lebanese emirate.

930.name: Emirate of Mount Lebanon
930.description: The golden age of Lebanese semi-autonomy under Fakhreddine II and the Shihab emirs, the emergence of a distinct Lebanese identity, and the sectarian conflicts that ended the emirate system.

sub_clusters.name: Fakhreddine II and the Ma'n Emirate
sub_clusters.description: Emir Fakhreddine II's unification of Mount Lebanon and parts of coastal Syria, his alliance with Tuscany, modernizing reforms, and ultimate execution by the Ottomans.
key_events: Fakhreddine II extends Ma'n control from Beirut to Palmyra, creating a proto-Lebanese state (1590–1633)
Ottomans capture and execute Fakhreddine II in Istanbul (1635)

sub_clusters.name: Shihab Emirate and Sectarian Conflict
sub_clusters.description: The Shihab dynasty's succession to the Ma'ns, Bashir II's long reign, the Egyptian occupation under Ibrahim Pasha, and the eruption of Druze-Maronite sectarian violence.
key_events: Bashir II allies with Egypt's Ibrahim Pasha against the Ottomans (1831–1840)
Druze-Maronite sectarian conflict leads to the end of the emirate system (1840–1842)

930.name: Mutasarrifate of Mount Lebanon
930.description: The internationally guaranteed autonomous province of Mount Lebanon created after the 1860 massacres, governed by a Christian mutasarrif, and the seeds of modern Lebanon.

sub_clusters.name: 1860 Massacres and International Intervention
sub_clusters.description: The devastating Druze-Maronite civil war and massacres of 1860, French military intervention, and the creation of the autonomous Mutasarrifate under European guarantee.
key_events: Druze-Maronite massacres kill thousands, including in Damascus (1860)
Règlement Organique establishes the autonomous Mutasarrifate of Mount Lebanon (1861)

sub_clusters.name: Autonomy, Emigration, and WWI Famine
sub_clusters.description: The relative peace and prosperity of the Mutasarrifate, the great Lebanese diaspora to the Americas, the cultural nahda (renaissance), and the catastrophic Great Famine of Mount Lebanon during WWI.
key_events: Great Famine of Mount Lebanon — Ottoman blockade and locust plague kill an estimated 200,000 (1915–1918)

940.name: French Mandate and Independence
940.description: The creation of Greater Lebanon under French Mandate, the establishment of the confessional political system, and the struggle for independence during World War II.

sub_clusters.name: Creation of Greater Lebanon
sub_clusters.description: General Gouraud's proclamation of the State of Greater Lebanon, the annexation of Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon, the Bekaa, and southern regions to Mount Lebanon, and the 1926 Constitution.
key_events: General Gouraud proclaims the State of Greater Lebanon (September 1, 1920)
Lebanese Republic proclaimed with a constitution based on the French model (1926)

sub_clusters.name: Independence and National Pact
sub_clusters.description: The unwritten National Pact dividing power among sects, the independence crisis with French arrest of the government, national resistance, and the final withdrawal of French troops.
key_events: National Pact — unwritten agreement on confessional power-sharing (1943)
Lebanon declares independence; France arrests the government, provoking a crisis (November 1943)
Last French troops leave Lebanon (December 1946)

940.name: Golden Age and 1958 Crisis
940.description: Beirut's transformation into the 'Paris of the Middle East,' Lebanon's banking and tourism boom, the tensions of Arab nationalism, the Palestinian factor, and the 1958 crisis.

sub_clusters.name: Beirut — Paris of the Middle East
sub_clusters.description: Lebanon's post-independence economic boom, Beirut as a cosmopolitan center of banking, publishing, and culture, and the 1958 crisis when US Marines landed to support the government.
key_events: 1958 Lebanon crisis — US Marines land in Beirut (Operation Blue Bat) to stabilize the government

sub_clusters.name: Palestinian Presence and Rising Tensions
sub_clusters.description: The Cairo Agreement granting PLO autonomy in Lebanon, Israeli reprisal raids, the growing Palestinian military presence, and the deepening sectarian fissures leading to civil war.
key_events: Cairo Agreement grants PLO control over Palestinian camps in Lebanon (1969)

950.name: Lebanese Civil War
950.description: The devastating fifteen-year civil war involving multiple factions, foreign interventions by Syria, Israel, and multinational forces, and the near-total destruction of Beirut.

sub_clusters.name: Outbreak and Syrian Intervention
sub_clusters.description: The Ain al-Rummaneh bus incident sparking civil war, the partition of Beirut, the Tal al-Zaatar massacre, the Syrian intervention of 1976, and the escalation of sectarian violence.
key_events: Ain al-Rummaneh bus incident triggers the civil war (April 13, 1975)
Syrian forces enter Lebanon (1976)

sub_clusters.name: Israeli Invasion and Multinational Force
sub_clusters.description: Israel's 1982 invasion reaching Beirut, the siege and PLO evacuation, the Sabra and Shatila massacre, the multinational peacekeeping force, and the devastating Marine barracks bombing.
key_events: Israel invades Lebanon — Operation Peace for Galilee (June 1982)
Sabra and Shatila massacre of Palestinian refugees (September 1982)
Suicide bombing of US Marine barracks kills 241 Americans (October 23, 1983)

sub_clusters.name: Final Phase and Taif Accord
sub_clusters.description: The War of the Camps, Michel Aoun's 'War of Liberation' against Syria, the Taif Accord rebalancing the confessional system, and the end of hostilities.
key_events: Taif Accord signed, restructuring Lebanon's political system (1989)
Syrian forces oust General Aoun; civil war ends (October 1990)

960.name: Post-War Reconstruction and Syrian Withdrawal
960.description: Rafik Hariri's reconstruction of Beirut, Syrian political domination, the 2005 Cedar Revolution following Hariri's assassination, and the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war.

sub_clusters.name: Hariri Era and Reconstruction
sub_clusters.description: Prime Minister Rafik Hariri's Solidere project rebuilding downtown Beirut, the continued Syrian military and political presence, and the assassination of Hariri by car bomb.
key_events: Solidere begins reconstruction of Beirut's central district (1994)
Assassination of former PM Rafik Hariri (February 14, 2005)

sub_clusters.name: Cedar Revolution and 2006 War
sub_clusters.description: The massive Cedar Revolution protests forcing Syrian withdrawal, the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war devastating southern Lebanon and Beirut's southern suburbs, and the ongoing political paralysis.
key_events: Cedar Revolution — Syrian forces withdraw from Lebanon after 29 years (April 2005)
2006 Lebanon War — 34-day Israel-Hezbollah conflict (July–August 2006)

960.name: Economic Collapse and Crisis
960.description: The Syrian refugee crisis, the total collapse of Lebanon's banking system and economy, the catastrophic Beirut port explosion, and the country's descent into state failure.

sub_clusters.name: Syrian Refugee Crisis and Political Paralysis
sub_clusters.description: The influx of over one million Syrian refugees, the presidential vacuum lasting over two years, Hezbollah's intervention in the Syrian Civil War, and the garbage crisis protests.

sub_clusters.name: Financial Collapse and Beirut Explosion
sub_clusters.description: The October 2019 revolution, the financial system's total collapse wiping out savings, the devastating Beirut port explosion of 2020, hyperinflation, and the ongoing multi-dimensional crisis.
key_events: October 17 Revolution — nationwide protests against corruption and sectarianism (2019)
Beirut port explosion — 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate devastate the city, killing 218 (August 4, 2020)
Lebanese pound loses over 90% of its value in economic meltdown (2020–2023)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
